p: Highway 287 between Fort Collins and Laramie has two moods in January. On Monday morning it was in the bad one: wind out of the west, snow moving sideways across the road in long white ropes, a pickup in the ditch near the state line with its flashers on and nobody in it.

Maria drove it at 5:40 AM with the radio off. On the passenger seat were two sets of scrubs, her badge, a stethoscope she hadn't used in four years and had brought anyway, and a printed copy of Walt Hagen's complaint. She'd read it enough times to know it by heart. Forty-seven clicks, up from forty-one.

She knew where the six new clicks had come from. A screen that made the discharging doctor confirm he'd seen every result still pending. A count of medications on every transfer, so a list that came up short would get noticed. Both came out of the Laramie review in December. Both were good ideas. Both were hers.
The plan for the week fit on an index card. Laramie Monday through Wednesday. Rawlins Thursday. Cheyenne Friday. No slides, no town halls. Scrubs, a legal pad, and the night shift's coffee.

Laramie's med-surg charge nurse met her at the elevator at 6:50. Renee had twenty years on the unit and the posture of someone who'd been told a vice president was coming and had decided to reserve judgment. She handed Maria a handheld scanner, still warm from the charger.
Wristband first, Maria said. Then the med. Then you look at the patient anyway.
Renee nodded once, which seemed to settle something. Then you can follow Jess at nine. And Dr. Hagen's waiting for you in the surgeons' lounge. He's been there since seven. He brought a pencil.

Walt Hagen was in the surgeons' lounge with the complaint, a pencil, and a printed discharge summary with tally marks down the margin. Forty-seven, he said. I counted again this morning, in case you thought I was exaggerating.

He walked her through the new ones. A screen to confirm he'd seen every pending result. Two clicks to acknowledge each one. A medication count to confirm on transfers. She knew all six. She'd sat in the room where they were decided.
I'm told these were safety fixes. I believe it. I'd like to know which of my forty-seven are keeping someone safe, and which are keeping someone covered.

She follows him through a gallbladder discharge at ten, legal pad on her knee. Each click gets one word: safety, billing, legal, habit, nothing. The pending results check stays, and he agrees it should. Kiran folds its two acknowledgments into one signed list, and an old duplicate diagnosis entry goes. Walt looks at the new count for a long time. You kept the ones that matter and told me why. That's new. At the door he turns. While you're counting, count the nurses.
Monday afternoon Renee pulled up an order on the MedaLink screen and turned it toward Maria without a word.
It read: insulin regular 6U SubQ AC. Below it, warfarin 5.0 mg PO QD.
Night shift read the first one as sixty last spring, Renee said. Pharmacy caught it. The doctor didn't type it like that. He picked it off a list. They're all built like that.

Kiran checked from Fort Collins while she waited. Laramie's order sentence library, built in 2011, had 312 sentences with a U, a QD, a QOD, or a trailing zero. About 140 active orders had been written from them.

Aisha puts it on the next council agenda as urgent. Pharmacy and nursing review the list in a week: U becomes units, QD becomes daily, trailing zeros go. Kiran builds, and pharmacy checks each sentence. Then pharmacy rewrites the 140 active orders one by one, and Renee tapes the old screenshot inside the med room door with a line through it.

Tuesday at nine Maria followed Jess, a nurse five years out of school, on her morning med pass. Six patients, twenty-two doses. Jess scanned the wristband, scanned each medication, and MedaLink checked them against the eMAR. Green, green, green.

Room 312's wristband had been through two days of hand sanitizer and a shower. The scanner beeped and failed. Jess tried twice, then clicked a button at the bottom of the eMAR labeled Given, no scan. The dose was charted. She was on to the next one in ten seconds.

Everybody uses it when the band won't read, Jess said. Scanning's six clicks when it works. That button is two. The night nurses built it, years ago. She didn't sound defensive. She sounded like someone describing the weather.

She asks Jess to read the five rights on that dose, out loud, against the eMAR. All right. She has the unit reprint 312's band before the next dose. Then she keeps walking and keeps a tally. Five of twenty-two doses skip the scan: three bands that won't read, a liquid from pharmacy with no barcode, a scanner battery that dies in 316. At the end Jess looks wary. You're not writing me up? I'm fixing the bands, Maria says. And the button.
Tuesday afternoon Walt found her in the cafeteria and set a printed note on her tray, face down. On the back, in pencil, were tally marks.
You counted my clicks. I counted your nurses. Two days on my floor. Fifty-eight doses I watched. Eleven went through that button.
He'd brought the monthly quality report from the unit break room, too.

BCMA scan compliance, December, as reported. Percent of doses with both the wristband and the medication scanned, from the monthly quality report. The three MedaLink hospitals report the highest rates in the system.
Your oldest system has your best numbers, Walt said. In my line of work, when the chart looks better than the patient, you look again.

Kiran pulls December at Laramie, every dose and every path it took into the chart. It takes him until midnight, and he doesn't mention that. Walt counted one in five going around the scanner. The data says one in six. Close enough, Walt says when she tells him. I'm a surgeon, not a statistician.

Wednesday at 7:40 Maria sat at the surgery unit desk beside Pat, the unit clerk, who'd held the job for twenty-six years. A stack of paper came up from the OR. Post-op orders, handwritten on a preprinted form, signed. Pat typed them into MedaLink one at a time and picked the surgeon's name as the ordering provider.
Dr. Hagen's, Pat said, holding one up. Best handwriting in the building.
Cascade's annual report to the board listed all eleven hospitals as CPOE live. Kiran checked. It is live, he said. Surgery just doesn't use it much.

Kiran pulls it: last quarter, 38 percent of Laramie surgical orders were entered by the prescriber. Maria sends Ochoa the number with two lines on what CPOE means. He puts it in the next board report as written. Then she asks Walt why he writes on paper. The post-op order set is thirty-four clicks. Paper takes forty seconds. She writes that down too.

Kiran found it Wednesday night. MedaLink's BCMA report had been built in 2016 by an analyst long gone. It divided scanned doses by doses charted through the scanning screen. The Given, no scan button, built by Laramie's night nurses that same year, charted doses through a different screen. The report had never seen them.
Laramie, December: the report said 97 percent. Counting every dose given, it was 81.
Both numbers are real, Kiran said. One of them just answers a question nobody asked. The next report was due to the board's quality committee on February 1.

The nursing quality director owns the metric. The director, the three CNOs, and Kiran agree on one definition: scanned doses over every dose charted, by any path. The February report shows both rates for December side by side, with a paragraph on why. The committee asks hard questions, and Ochoa answers them beside her. Nobody's number dropped. It had always been 81.
Thursday morning I-80 was closed between Laramie and Rawlins, blowing snow at Elk Mountain and a jackknifed truck. Rawlins would have to be a video call.

So Maria had a free morning in Laramie and a conference room with a long blank wall. Jess and Renee came in on their break, with a pharmacist from downstairs. Kiran joined on a laptop propped against the coffee pot. She wanted to see the whole medication process at Laramie in one place before anyone fixed a piece of it.

Five lanes on butcher paper: surgeon, clerk, pharmacy, cabinet, nurse. Paper order, typed in, verified, pulled, scanned, given, charted. Then the diamonds. The band that won't read and the arrow down to Given, no scan. The liquid with no barcode. The pharmacist who isn't there at night, so the cabinet runs on override. By noon the wall shows three places where a dose goes around the scanner. Renee takes a photo. First time anybody drew it the way we do it.
The Rawlins CNO, Gail, came on the video call that afternoon from her office, with a window behind her full of snow. We'd have loved to have you. The road had other plans.

Rawlins had twenty-two beds and one doctor in the building at night. We haven't had a night pharmacist since last January, Gail said. After five o'clock the nurses pull first doses from the cabinet on override, and a Cheyenne pharmacist reviews the night's orders in the morning.

I know it's not ideal, Gail said. But our scan rate's the best in the system. Ninety-eight. We're careful. She'd found a telepharmacy company online that could verify orders overnight, and she wanted to know if Maria would sign off.

Cascade's pharmacy director takes it on. Cheyenne already has a pharmacist overnight. With access to Rawlins orders in MedaLink and the state pharmacy board's rules checked, remote verification can start in March. Night first doses will get a pharmacist's eyes before the cabinet opens. Gail is quiet a second. We asked for this two years ago. Maria believes her.

Friday, Cheyenne. Denise Harmon met her at the elevator. You're in my building. I hear you've been counting things. Denise had led the nurses against Penwright two years ago and ended up its best champion. Now she was a One Chart superuser, and she'd read the draft frequency map Kiran's team sent out for review.

You mapped MedaLink BID to Corvane BID. Up here BID means nine and nine. Breakfast and bedtime. Down there BID is nine and five, so the evening dose lands at dinner. And half our q12h drugs were built as BID in 2014 because it was easier. Map those by name and you just moved every med pass on my floor, and you changed when people's heparin is due.
Maria's phone buzzed while Denise was still talking.
A text from Lucia. mom is BID the same as q12h. my practice quiz says no and i think the quiz is wrong

Pharmacy pulls every active frequency at the three hospitals, and each one is mapped by what it means: how many doses, at what times, and whether the timing matters. Fourteen MedaLink BID orders turn out to be q12h drugs and get mapped that way. The question of standard times goes to the council. Denise reads the final map and signs it. Now that I'll train.

Friday afternoon, in Denise's office, Kiran came on speakerphone. To size the One Chart training plan, he needed one number per hospital: average daily census. It would set how many superusers each unit needed at the elbow on go-live weekend, and how many scanners to order.
He had three reports and three numbers for Rawlins in December. Finance said ten. Nursing's staffing report said fourteen. The bed board said sixteen.

Gail called in from Rawlins. They're all real. We just count different heads. Finance counts acute inpatients. We count the swing beds too, because we staff them. The bed board counts observation patients, because they're in a bed.

Finance, nursing, and HIM agree in one call: inpatient days count acute and swing bed patients, observation is reported separately. It goes in writing. Rawlins is fourteen, and its plan adds support for the observation patients the nurses chart on too. Every hospital uses the same rule.

Tuesday, January 26, Aisha called while Maria was eating lunch at her desk. Her sepsis alert was going to the council next week, and she wanted a baseline: order to first dose of antibiotics, all eleven hospitals.

Kiran had the data and a problem. In Corvane, the time given came from the scan. At the MedaLink hospitals, Given, no scan let the nurse type in the time. One Laramie record showed an antibiotic given two minutes before it was ordered.
Just give me the average, Aisha said. I need one number for the council.

The clock starts when the order is signed and stops when the first dose is charted. Median, plus the 90th percentile, because sepsis kills the patients who wait longest. Typed-in times show up in their own column. Laramie's median is 74 minutes by scan and 51 by typed time, and nobody believes the 51. Aisha studies it. So the button's in my data too. It's in everybody's, Maria says.
Thursday, January 28. The restated report would go to the committee on Monday. Kiran wanted to go further: the true rate at all three MedaLink hospitals, month by month, for the past year.
He had an idea to make it faster. The dispensing cabinets log every removal with a time and a patient. Cleaner than MedaLink. I could just count those as the doses given.

Kiran builds it in the warehouse: every eMAR dose by how it was charted, joined to cabinet removals to find doses pulled and never charted, and charted and never pulled. It takes him four nights. He sends the file at 11:52 PM on Monday, February 1, with no message at all.

Maria drove home from Cheyenne on Friday night with the heater on high and five days of notes on the seat beside her. Forty-seven clicks. Three hundred and twelve order sentences. Five of twenty-two doses. A wall of butcher paper. Fourteen heparin orders. Most of it was the same lesson from different directions. The system said one thing and the floor did another, and nobody had looked closely enough to see the space between.

Somewhere past Wellington she worked out why the week had gone well. She'd let other people show her things. A nurse showed her a button. A surgeon showed her a tally. A nurse manager in Cheyenne showed her a map that was wrong. She'd spent fourteen years being the one who knew. This week she'd been the one who asked, and she'd learned more.
Walt emailed the day after the restated report went out, which Renee said he never did. Saw the restated report. 81. Thank you for looking again. My complaint stands. I'll grant that you looked.
Lucia was on the couch when she got in, the practice quiz still open on her laptop. You never answered me. BID and q12h.
Your quiz is right, Maria said, and sat down next to her. BID is twice a day, when the hospital says. q12h is every twelve hours, no matter what. Some drugs don't care. Some do. Heparin cares.

Lucia clicked to the next question. Maria watched her for a while, the pencil behind her ear, the way she mouthed the words. Five days of asking people about their work, and she'd never asked her own daughter about hers.
Lucia thought about it. You come home tired, she said. You never come home sorry you went.
Maria didn't have anything to say to that. She leaned over and pointed at the next question, and Lucia knew that one too.
Kiran's file arrived at 11:52 PM on Monday, February 1. She opened it at 5:50 the next morning, before her one-on-one with Ochoa, with the coffee still brewing.
The Laramie and Cheyenne lines looked the way she expected. Laramie sat around 81 all year. Cheyenne ran in the low 90s, and Denise's floor was higher.
Rawlins BCMA scan compliance, counting every dose. The true rate, from the eMAR, by month. The report the board saw said 98 percent every month.

Ninety in December 2025. Sixty-four in January. It had never come back. For a whole year, more than one dose in three at Rawlins had gone around the scanner, and every month the report had said ninety-eight, and Gail had been proud of it, and so had everyone who read it.
Maria sat very still. Then she remembered Gail on the video call, a window full of snow behind her, saying it almost in passing. We haven't had a night pharmacist since last January.
She picked up her phone and called Kiran, who answered on the first ring at six in the morning, which told her he hadn't slept either.
I know, he said. A year.
